newsitem.title: JORDAN: Internet fever sweeps Jordan, government is online.
newsitem.headline: Internet fever sweeps Jordan, government is online.

text.p: Jordan's English-speaking elite is meeting the government online, posing tough questions on corruption, human rights and controversial peace with Israel.
This may not appear earth-shaking in the free-wheeling West, but in conservative Jordan it is a major event and a staple for conversation in trendy restaurants and high-class parties.

Royal family members logging in under first names are among 1,500 subscribers in NETS, a Jordanian-owned online service offering various conferences, including "Ask the government", a forum where residents can talk to officials directly.

NETS users, equipped with computers and modems, lob blunt policy questions at the government and vent anger at the October 1994 peace treaty with Israel or King Hussein's year-old shift in policy towards Iraq, once a major Arab ally.
Others complain about the Israeli and other embassies for refusing to give them visas and demand government intervention.

On most occasions, Information Minister Marwan Muasher and Bassem Awadallah, economic adviser to Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti, answer back -- sometimes admitting shortcomings, criticising questioners or ignoring them.
Jordan's much-feared General Intelligence Department joined NETS last month and said it welcomed queries.

King Hussein, who began democratic reforms in 1989, is getting some credit for it, officials and operators say. He and his aides might have realised they would be better off trying to make use of the electronic revolution than resisting it.

"We are the only government in the Middle East that is online, receiving uncensored questions and comments from NETS users," Awadallah told Reuters in an interview. "And we respond to them to the best of our ability."
This forum began in April after U.S.-educated Kabariti, 46, formed his government and promised more openness to the public.
Prince Hamzah and Prince Hashem, King Hussein's younger sons, express their views on another NETS forum tackling issues that might improve the socio-economic and political climate.

Two days of unrest that flared in the southern town of Karak in August and spread to nearby towns after Kabariti doubled bread prices under IMF-agreed economic reforms became a hot issue on the NETS forum called "A Better Jordan".
The opposition said rising economic hardship caused the trouble, which the king and his government blamed on Iraq.
Prince Hamzah, 16, criticised some Jordanians who torched some state buildings and private banks during the unrest, saying Jordan was "target of a well-planned and executed conspiracy".
But subscriber Ziad al-Nabulsi disagreed. "It did not need a genius to predict that tampering with bread prices would result in public uproar...."
Jordan appears to be leading the Arab world in free uses of electronic media, operators say.

Gulf states Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Oman have Internet access, but their governments control the service to shield their conservative societies from temptation brought in by the free information superhighway.
NETS, six other online firms selling different web openings, and Global One/Sprint Jordan, the kingdom's Internet provider, are privately owned but operating under official licensing.

Sprint Jordan General Manager Imad Ayoub insists he feels no pressure to censor Jordanians from surfing through such powderkeg topics as sex and atheism -- taboo subjects -- and says there are no plans to restrict access to any sites.
Its club of 1,000 subscribers is steadily growing -- 60 percent of clients are businessmen and the rest individuals -- who pay fees ranging from $40 to $85 a month depending on use.
But he and others agree it will affect the relatively closed culture as did the high-tech satellite dishes sweeping Jordan.
"Internet is going to affect the culture as it is very open and has no limits on information it shows," said Ayoub.

"But technically speaking, there is no good way to prevent anyone from seeing anything that is on Internet," he said. In many Gulf states, users are sidestepping restriction on Internet by using long-distance services to cybersurf.
NETS general manager Marwan Juma says subscribers have to respect certain rules or else membership will be suspended.
He wants the "Ask the Government" experiment to succeed in a region where most states are not on public discourse, placing limits on what can be published or even talked about.

"The two main rules are: you can't attack another subscriber or a public figure personally," said Juma. "So far, we have had no problems, but every once in a while, I have to come in and say: Come on guys, keep it down."
NETS, which has more than 40 public forums and costs $15 a month, plans to add Arabic onlines to broaden its popular base and wants more ministries and schools to join.

While impoverished Jordan may be among the region's most advanced in the computer use, the use of electronic media remains limited because of lack of information on Internet use and high costs for purchasing a computer and a modum.
Most of Jordan's dozen universities were not Internet-wired because they lacked technical capabilities and know-how.
Ayoub's best Internet users are young people.
"The younger generation are picking it up faster. But most kids do not have computers, therefore we are going to universities and putting it there to get the masses on to it."
